title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the basket cookie
description: The basket cookie is entirely controlled by the client, but it is passed directly to pickle.loads(). A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the web application's process whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
evidence: read_basket() obtains request.cookies['basket'] at line 16, base64-decodes it, and calls pickle.loads(raw) at line 20 without a signature or integrity check; /basket is unauthenticated and invokes read_basket() at line 46.

title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
description: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and uses the untrusted sub claim to select the account for which it issues a newly signed token. An attacker can submit a token with the sub of another user, including a staff user, and obtain a valid session for that account.
evidence: refresh() calls jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}) at line 101, loads the user from claims.get('sub') at line 104, and returns make_token(user) at line 107 without ever verifying the original token.

title: Authenticated users can read other customers' orders
description: The order detail endpoint authenticates the caller but does not enforce that the requested order belongs to that caller. Any logged-in user who guesses an order ID can read another customer's order contents, payment totals, delivery information, and refunds.
evidence: show_order() calls order_json(get_order(order_id)) at line 49; unlike own_order(), get_order() only checks that the order exists and never compares customer_id with g.user.

title: Product search concatenates the query into SQL
description: The unauthenticated search endpoint inserts the q parameter directly into a SQL statement. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause or inject additional SQL syntax, potentially exposing or modifying database data depending on the SQLite statement parser and execution context.
evidence: The query at line 41 is built with "... LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." rather than a bound parameter.

title: Customer review report is injectable through display names
description: The admin report interpolates a customer's mutable display name into SQL. A customer can choose a display name containing SQL syntax, then a staff member viewing that customer's report causes the injected expression to execute.
evidence: update_account() permits user-controlled display_name values, and reviews_by_customer() constructs `WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'` with an f-string at line 80 instead of binding the value.

title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, and the product page renders that text with the Jinja safe filter. A malicious review can therefore execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser.
evidence: add_review() stores the submitted body without HTML sanitization at shopapi/products.py:90-91, while product.html renders r.body|safe at line 13.

title: Payment-status timeouts are treated as successful payments
description: If the payment provider times out, the endpoint assumes the payment was paid and moves the order to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A transient timeout or provider/network interference can therefore let an unpaid order proceed as paid.
evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 assigns status = 'paid', and lines 43-45 then set status to processing and paid_pence to total_pence.

title: Payment webhook does not validate the settled amount
description: A signed paid event can mark an order processing with any amount_pence, including zero or an amount below the order total. The signature covers only the order ID, so it does not protect the status or amount fields from tampering by anyone able to produce or replay a valid order-ID signature.
evidence: webhook_signature() signs only str(order_id) at lines 53-55; payment_webhook() accepts event status and amount independently and writes int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) to paid_pence at lines 69-71 without comparing it to order.total_pence.

title: Production JWT signing key is hard-coded in source
description: The application uses a fixed secret embedded in the repository for HS256 JWT signing. Anyone who obtains the source can forge arbitrary access tokens, including staff tokens; the configuration does not require an externally supplied key.
evidence: SECRET_KEY is assigned the literal value "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" at line 3 and is used by jwt.encode/jwt.decode in shopapi/auth.py:27 and 42.

title: Authentication failures are swallowed by the auth decorator
description: require_auth catches the abort(401) raised for missing or invalid credentials and continues into the endpoint with g.user set to None. Endpoints that do not independently use g.user can therefore be reached without authentication; the gift-card balance endpoint is one such case and exposes card balances to anonymous callers.
evidence: The decorator catches Exception around abort(401) at lines 52-58 and always calls f(*args, **kwargs) at line 58. giftcards.balance() has only @require_auth and returns the card balance at shopapi/giftcards.py:10-16 without checking g.user.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashes use a single unsalted SHA-256 digest, which is inexpensive to brute-force and enables identical passwords to be identified. A database disclosure would make the application's user passwords substantially easier to crack than with a password-specific KDF.
evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at line 16; no salt or work-factor KDF is used.

title: Image import follows redirects outside the approved host allowlist
description: The initial URL is restricted to approved public hosts, but requests.get follows redirects by default and the redirected destination is never revalidated. A compromised approved host or redirect can make the staff-only importer fetch internal or otherwise unintended resources.
evidence: check_url() validates only the original URL at lines 28-35, then requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) at line 50 follows redirects without allowlist or destination validation.
